author: Marcus Minucius Felix

passages.original: omitto illos rudes et ueteres, qui de suis dictis sapientes esse meruerunt. sit Thales Milesius omnium primus, qui primus omnium de caelestibus disputauit. is autem Milesius Thales rerum initium aquam dixit, deum autem eam mentem quae ex aqua cuncta formauerit: [eo altior et sublimior aquae et spiritus ratio, quam ut ab homine potuerit inueniri, a deo traditum] : uides philosophi principalis nobiscum penitus opinionem consonare.
passages.english: I pass over those rough and ancient men who earned the name of wise for their sayings. Let Thales of Miletus be first of all, who first of all debated about heavenly things. This Thales of Miletus said that the origin of things was water, and that God was that mind which formed all things out of water: [an account of water and spirit too lofty and sublime to have been discovered by man; it was handed down by God]. You see that the opinion of the chief philosopher agrees with ours entirely.
passages.notes: The bracketed clause is marked by the edition as a probable interpolation; its grammar is defective ("traditum" does not agree with "ratio"; the construction "eo altior ... quam ut" lacks a main verb).

passages.original: eadem fere Chrysippus: uim diuinam, rationalem naturam et mundum interim et fatalem necessitatem deum credit Zenonemque interpretatione physiologica in Hesiodi, Homeri Orpheique carminibus imitatur.
passages.english: Chrysippus says much the same: he believes that God is a divine force, a rational nature, and at times the world, and fated necessity; and he imitates Zeno in his physical interpretation of the poems of Hesiod, Homer and Orpheus.

passages.original: loquitur Plato: partes orbis nunc inundare dicit, nunc alternis uicibus ardescere, et cum ipsum mundum perpetuum et insolubilem diceret esse fabricatum, addidit tamen, ipsi artifici Deo soli et solubilem et esse mortalem.
passages.english: Plato speaks: he says that parts of the world are now flooded, now in alternate turns set ablaze; and though he said that the world itself was made everlasting and indissoluble, he nevertheless added that to God alone, its maker himself, it is both dissoluble and mortal.
passages.notes: The passage appears to belong to the Stoics rather than Plato in the usual order of this text; the text may be displaced or corrupt here. "ipsi artifici Deo soli" is taken as "to God alone, the maker himself", i.e. that it can be dissolved by God.
